## Summary from last lecture

::: med-space
:::

Linear models as a unified framework:

-   **Regression**: numeric explanatory variable

-   **ANOVA/t-test**: categorical explanatory variables

-   **ANCOVA**: numeric and categorical explanatory variables

## The problem with ANOVA {.smaller}

::: med-space
:::

```{r}
penguins %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g, fill = species)) +
  geom_jitter(alpha = .75, shape = 21) +
  geom_pointrange(
    stat = "summary",
    fun.data = mean_sdl,
    show.legend = FALSE,
    shape = 21
  ) +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Body mass (g)"
  ) +
  scale_fill_colorblind() +
  theme_classic(base_size = 20) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

## The problem with ANOVA {.smaller}

::: med-space
:::

```{r}
#| echo: true

m_spec <- lm(body_mass_g ~ species, data = penguins)
anova(m_spec)
```

::: med-space
:::

::: question
ANOVA tells us: "**There is a difference** between species"

But **which** species differs from which other?
:::

## Multiple comparisons {.smaller}

::: med-space
:::

For 3 species, we have 3 possible comparisons:

-   Adelie vs. Chinstrap
-   Adelie vs. Gentoo
-   Chinstrap vs. Gentoo

::: med-space
:::

::: fragment
::: question
Why not just do 3 models?
:::
:::

## Alpha error inflation {.smaller}

::: med-space
:::

::::: columns
::: column
-  Each test has a 5% error risk (α = 0.05)

::: fragment
-  **Probability of making no error in 1 test:** 0.95
:::

::: fragment
-  **Probability of making no error in 3 tests:** $0.95 \times 0.95 \times 0.95 = 0.857$
:::

::: fragment
-   **Probability of making at least 1 error:** $1 - 0.857 = 0.143 = 14.3\%$
:::
:::

::: column
::: fragment

::: med-space
:::

```{r}
#| fig-height: 10

n_comparisons <- 1:20
error_rate <- 1 - (0.95^n_comparisons)

data.frame(
  n = n_comparisons,
  error = error_rate
) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = error)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.5, color = "darkred") +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "darkred") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(
    x = "Number of comparisons",
    y = "Probability of at least 1 error"
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 23)
```

:::
:::
:::::

## Family-wise error rate (FWER) {.smaller}

::: med-space
:::

> 
**FWER:** The probability of making at least one type I error in a set of tests


::: small
| Number of groups | Number of comparisons | FWER (no correction) |
|-------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| 2                 | 1                      | 5.0%                   |
| 3                 | 3                      | 14.3%                  |
| 4                 | 6                      | 26.5%                  |
| 5                 | 10                     | 40.1%                  |
| 10                | 45                     | 90.0%                  |
:::

::: med-space
:::
::: med-space
:::

::: question
We need to adjust our p-values to control the FWER
:::

## p-value adjustments {.smaller}

::: med-space
:::
::: small
| Method              | Description                                | When to use           |
|----------------------|--------------------------------------------|----------------------------|
| **Bonferroni**       | Divides α by number of tests              | Simple, few tests       |
| **Holm-Bonferroni**  | Sequential Bonferroni (less strict)      | Alternative to Bonferroni   |
| **Benjamini-Hochberg** | Controls false discovery rate | Many tests          |
| **Tukey HSD**        | Accounts for all comparisons   | **Multiple comparisons**     |
:::

::: med-space
:::

::: question
Tukey tests are often used for post-hoc tests 
:::

## Post-hoc Tests in `R` {.smaller}

::: med-space
:::


```{r}
#| echo: true

m_spec <- lm(body_mass_g ~ species, data = penguins)

estimate_contrasts(m_spec, p_adjust = "tukey")
```


## Visualise Post-Hoc Tests {.smaller}

::: med-space
:::


::: {.columns}
::: {.column}
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

estimate_means(m_spec, by = "species") %>%
  plot()
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

estimate_means(m_spec, by = "species") %>%
  plot() +
  theme_light(base_size = 21)
```


:::
::: {.column .small}


#### Recommendation

-   Plot 95% CI

    >
   "**95% Confidence Interval:** is a range calculated such that, if repeated many times, 95% of such intervals would contain the true parameter value."

-   **No overlap:** Groups are statistiaclly significantly different (p < .05)

-   **Overlap:** May be statistically significantly different, but effect is likely small
:::
:::

::: med-space
:::

::: {.fragment .question .small}
Recently, researchers are moving away from p-values as hard cutoffs. Effect size (biological importance) matters more than p < .05!
:::

## Part 2: Linear model assumptions {background-color="#440154"}

::: med-space
:::

::: center-align
::: huge
**When can we use a linear model?**
:::
:::

## The three key assumptions {.smaller}

::: med-space
:::



::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="33%"}
#### 1. Independence

Observations are independent of each other
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
#### 2. Homoscedasticity

Residual variance is constant



:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
#### 3. Normality

Residuals follow a normal distribution
:::
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="33%"}

![](images/moorea_mpa.png){height="260"}

:::
::: {.column width="33%"}

```{r}
#| fig-height: 9

set.seed(123)
n <- 200
x <- runif(n, 0, 10)
y <- 2 + 3 * x + rnorm(n, 0, 0.5 * (2 + 3 * x))

df_hetero <- tibble(x = x, y = y)

ggplot(df_hetero, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "darkred") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(
    x = "x",
    y = "y"
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 26)
```

:::
::: {.column width="33%"}

```{r}
#| fig-height: 9

set.seed(456)
n <- 200
x2 <- runif(n, 0, 10)
y2 <- 5 + 2 * x2 + rexp(n, rate = 0.5)

df_skew <- tibble(x = x2, y = y2)
m_skew <- lm(y ~ x, data = df_skew)

resid_df <- tibble(resid = residuals(m_skew))

ggplot(resid_df, aes(x = resid)) +
  geom_histogram(
    aes(y = after_stat(density)),
    bins = 30,
    fill = "lightblue",
    color = "black"
  ) +
  stat_function(
    fun = dnorm,
    args = list(mean = mean(resid_df$resid), sd = sd(resid_df$resid)),
    color = "red",
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Residuals",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 26)

```

:::
:::

## Assumption 1: Independence {.smaller}

::: med-space
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column}


#### Observations are independent

*Violation = one observation influences another*

-   Repeated measures of the same individuals
-   Spatial impact
-   Pseudoreplication
-   Hierarchical structure (sites, populations)

:::
::: {.column}
::: fragment
#### Consequences

-   Underestimation of standard error
-   Confidence intervals too narrow
-   p-values too small

::: question
These are serious consequences!
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Assumption 2: Homoscedasticity {.smaller}

::: med-space
:::

::::: columns
::: column
```{r}
#| fig-height: 7

set.seed(123)
x <- runif(100, 0, 10)
y_homo <- 2 + 3 * x + rnorm(100, 0, 2)

data.frame(x = x, y = y_homo) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "darkred", se = F) +
  labs(
    title = "Homoscedasticity",
    x = "Predictor",
    y = "Response"
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 26)
```

<div style="text-align: center;">
**Constant variance**
</div>

:::
::: column
```{r}
#| fig-height: 7

y_hetero <- 2 + 3 * x + rnorm(100, 0, 0.5 * (2 + 3 * x))

data.frame(x = x, y = y_hetero) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "darkred", se = F) +
  labs(
    title = "Heteroscedasticity",
    x = "Predictor",
    y = "Response"
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 26)
```

<div style="text-align: center;">
**Variance increases**
</div>

:::
:::::

$$
\begin{align}
y_i &\sim \mathrm{Normal}(\mu_i,~{\color{#D81B60}{\sigma}}) \\
\mu_i &= a + b x_i
\end{align}
$$



## Assumption 2: Homoscedasticity {.smaller}
::: med-space
:::

::::: columns
::: column
**Examples**

-   Variance increases with the mean
-   Count data (abundance)
-   Allometric processes
-   Body size and metabolism

:::

::: column
::: fragment
**Consequences**

-   Biased standard errors
-   CIs and tests less reliable
-   Less serious than non-independence

:::
:::
:::::

## Assumption 3: Normality of residuals {.smaller}

::: med-space
:::

#### **Residuals** (not raw data!) follow a normal distribution

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="75%"}
```{r}
# Calculate mean for regression line
mean_mass <- mean(penguins$body_mass_g)

# Create plot with residuals
penguins %>%
  filter(species == "Gentoo", ) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = body_mass_g)) +
  # Draw residual lines first (so they appear behind points)
  geom_segment(
    aes(xend = bill_length_mm, yend = fitted(lm(body_mass_g ~ bill_length_mm))),
    color = "darkred",
    linewidth = 0.5,
    alpha = 0.6
  ) +
  # Regression line
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "black", linewidth = 1.5) +
  # Data points
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "steelblue") +
  labs(
    x = "Bill length (mm)",
    y = "Body mass (g)"
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 20)
```


:::
::: {.column width="25%"}

$$
\begin{align}
y_i &\sim \mathrm{\color{#D81B60}{Normal}}(\mu_i,~{\sigma}) \\
\mu_i &= a + b x_i
\end{align}
$$

:::
:::


## Assumption 3: Normality of residuals {.smaller}

::: med-space
:::

::::: columns
::: column
**Examples**

-   Data strictly positive (heights, weights)
-   Percent data (between 0 and 100%)
-   Count data (abundance)
-   Probabilities (e.g. point-intercept transects)

:::

::: column
::: fragment
**Consequences**

-   Biased confidence intervals
-   p-values less reliable
-   Less serious than non-independence or severe heteroscedasticity

:::
:::
:::::


## Model Assessment

::: med-space
:::

::: question
Are assumptions violated? 

Can I get away with `lm()`?
:::

::: med-space
:::

Package `performance` helps to decide:

::: med-space
:::

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: slide

library(performance)

m_spec <- lm(body_mass_g ~ species, data = penguins)

check_model(m_spec)

```

## Model Assessment: Independence

::: med-space
:::

-   Not plot can help with that
-   Understand your data. 
   -   Any structure?
   -   Any correlated groups?
   -   Individuals measured multiple times?
   -   Spatial or temporal correlation?

## Model Assessment: Homoscedasticity

::: med-space
:::


```{r}
#| output: false

set.seed(123)
n <- 200


x_good <- runif(n, 5, 30)
y_good <- 0.5 + 0.8 * x_good + rnorm(n, 0, sd = 0.5) # Constant SD, no trend
m_good <- lm(y_good ~ x_good)

x_mild <- runif(n, 5, 30)
y_mild <- 0.5 + 0.8 * x_mild + rnorm(n, 0, sd = 0.2 + 0.2 * x_mild)
m_mild_hetero <- lm(y_mild ~ x_mild)

x_severe <- runif(n, 5, 30)
mean_count <- 1 + 0.6 * x_severe
y_severe <- rpois(n, lambda = pmax(mean_count, 0.1))
m_severe_hetero <- lm(y_severe ~ x_severe)

p_het1 <- plot(check_model(m_good, check = "homogeneity")) +
  theme_light(base_size = 16)
p_het2 <- plot(check_model(m_mild_hetero, check = "homogeneity"))
p_het3 <- plot(check_model(m_severe_hetero, check = "homogeneity"))

```


#### Homoscedastic 


```{r}
p_het1
```



## Model Assessment: Homoscedasticity

::: med-space
:::

#### Violation of Homoscedasticity 

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10

(p_het2 | p_het3) +
  plot_layout(ncol = 2)
```



## Model Assessment: Normality

::: med-space
:::

::::: columns
::: column
```{r}
#| fig-height: 12

# Histogram with normal curve
h_spec <- data.frame(resid = residuals(m_spec)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = resid)) +
  geom_histogram(
    aes(y = after_stat(density)),
    bins = 30,
    fill = "lightblue",
    color = "black"
  ) +
  stat_function(
    fun = dnorm,
    args = list(mean = 0, sd = sd(residuals(m_spec))),
    color = "red",
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of residuals", x = "Residuals", y = "Density") +
  theme_light(base_size = 26)

# Q-Q plot
q_spec <- check_normality(m_spec) %>%
  plot() +
  theme_light(base_size = 26)

# Stack histogram on top of Q-Q plot
h_spec / q_spec
```

:::

::: column

::: small

**Quantile-Quantile (QQ) plot**

-   Compares observed quantiles to theoretical quantiles of a normal distribution
-   If points follow the line: normal distribution
-   Deviations at extremes: heavy/light tails
-   S-pattern: skewness

:::
:::
:::::

## Model Assessment: Normality

::: med-space
:::


```{r}
set.seed(123)
n <- 400

# Normal distribution
normal_data <- rnorm(n)
m_normal <- lm(normal_data ~ 1)

# Heavy tails
heavy_tail <- rt(n, df = 1.8)
m_heavy <- lm(heavy_tail ~ 1)

# Skewed data
skewed <- rexp(n, rate = 1)
m_skewed <- lm(skewed ~ 1)

# Histogram + normal curve for normal data
h1 <- data.frame(resid = residuals(m_normal)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = resid)) +
  geom_histogram(
    aes(y = after_stat(density)),
    bins = 30,
    fill = "lightblue",
    color = "black"
  ) +
  stat_function(
    fun = dnorm,
    args = list(mean = 0, sd = sd(residuals(m_normal))),
    color = "red",
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  labs(title = "Normal distribution", x = "Residuals", y = "Density") +
  theme_light(base_size = 12)

# Q-Q plot for normal data
q1 <- check_normality(m_normal) %>%
  plot() +
  ylim(-1, 8) +
  labs(title = NULL) +
  theme_light(base_size = 12)

# Histogram for heavy tails
h2 <- data.frame(resid = residuals(m_heavy)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = resid)) +
  geom_histogram(
    aes(y = after_stat(density)),
    bins = 30,
    fill = "lightblue",
    color = "black"
  ) +
  stat_function(
    fun = dnorm,
    args = list(mean = 0, sd = sd(residuals(m_heavy))),
    color = "red",
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  labs(title = "Heavy tails", x = "Residuals", y = "Density") +
  theme_light(base_size = 12)

# Q-Q plot for heavy tails
q2 <- check_normality(m_heavy) %>%
  plot() +
  ylim(-1, 8) +
  labs(title = NULL) +
  theme_light(base_size = 12)

# Histogram for skewed data
h3 <- data.frame(resid = residuals(m_skewed)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = resid)) +
  geom_histogram(
    aes(y = after_stat(density)),
    bins = 30,
    fill = "lightblue",
    color = "black"
  ) +
  stat_function(
    fun = dnorm,
    args = list(mean = 0, sd = sd(residuals(m_skewed))),
    color = "red",
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  labs(title = "Positive skew", x = "Residuals", y = "Density") +
  theme_light(base_size = 12)

# Q-Q plot for skewed data
q3 <- check_normality(m_skewed) %>%
  plot() +
  ylim(-1, 8) +
  labs(title = NULL) +
  theme_light(base_size = 12)

# Arrange: histograms on top row, Q-Q plots on bottom row
(h1 | h2 | h3) / (q1 | q2 | q3)
```



## Actual Data {.smaller}

::: med-space
:::

-   Actual environmental data often violates at least one of these assumptions

-   Instead of doing non-parametric tests (forcing data into ranks, e.g. Wilcoxon, Kruskal Wallis, etc.), linear models can be extended


## Actual Data {.smaller}

::: med-space
:::


#### Advantages of linear models over non-parametric tests

-   Easier to **interpret**: The coefficients have actual biological meaning

-   We model the **actual data** (grams, meters, counts) instead of ranks (1st, 2nd, 3rd)

-   Include **interactions** (i.e. effect of one variables depends on other variable) are possible

-   Allow **predictions**

-   **Honest visualisations** with CI and effect size

## The three key assumptions {.smaller}

::: med-space
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="33%"}


#### 1. Independence

Observations are independent of each other

:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
#### 2. Homoscedasticity

Residual variance is constant

:::
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}
#### 3. Normality

Residuals follow a normal distribution
:::
:::
:::

::: med-space
:::

### If violated


::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="33%"}

Mixed effects models

(`glmmTMB` package)

:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
Variance structure 

(`nlme` & `glmmTMB` package)

:::
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}

::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}
**Generalized** linear models (GLMs)
